\item[Effect] Both implementations convert a numeral where its place fixes a
type and give it its default elsewhere.
So \EXP{x = 3} binds a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, and \EXP{x \sequiv z} is \VAR{true}
for \EXP{z\COLON\mathbb{Z}32 = 3} on both, where the compiled path answered
\VAR{false}; \EXP{y\COLON\mathbb{R}64 = 0.5} is strictly equivalent to
\EXP{a + a} for \EXP{a\COLON\mathbb{R}64 = 0.25}, \EXP{q\COLON\mathbb{Q} = 0.5}
binds \EXP{1/2}, and
\EXP{1/2 = 0.5} is \VAR{true}, where the interpreter answered otherwise
(rows~943 and~944 of the revival's gap ledger); a variable of type
\EXP{\mathbb{N}32} or \EXP{\mathbb{N}64} takes a numeral, and one of type
\EXP{\mathbb{R}32} takes a numeral with one rounding, where the interpreter
refused them (row~454); a variable bound from \EXP{3000000000} is a
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} and reaches a declaration over \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, where the
compiled path stopped at run time (row~946); \EXP{7} passed to a parameter of
type \TYP{Object} is a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} there (row~79); a numeral outside its
type's range is a static error, where the compiled path raised an exception at
run time (row~325); a numeral at a declared floating-point type is rounded once,
where the compiled code rounded it two or three times (row~862); and a
\KWD{nat} parameter used as a value is a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, which a variable of
type \EXP{\mathbb{N}32} refuses, where the compiled type checker took it
(row~486).
\EXP{\VAR{round}(2.50000000000000001)} is 2, its numeral read as an
\EXP{\mathbb{R}64}.
A numeral that took its default prints as a value of its default type, so that
\EXP{\hbox{\rm``''}\;2.50} is \hbox{\rm``\STR{2.5}''}, and the team's test
\nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/tests/NumberPrintTest.fss}, which asserted that a
numeral prints as written, is changed.
No value of a numeral type exists on either implementation when a program runs.
The compiled path, which until it is built on \library\ compiles against a
smaller library of its own, declares there the same numeral types, with
coercions generic over the four numbers from \TYP{NaturalNumeral} at its five
integer types and from \TYP{RadixPointNumeral} at \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} and
\EXP{\mathbb{R}32}; that library has no \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}.
The compiled code converts a numeral as written at a number type by that type's
coercion, whose body the compiler evaluates at the numeral's four numbers with
no knowledge of the type, into the constant that the class file holds; a value
of another representation, as one of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}}, and a value of a type of
a program's own come from one compiled method for each coercion from a numeral
type, which takes the four numbers as values of type \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} and which
each place calls once, in the initialization of the class of the component that
holds the place, before the program runs, the type's prefix \EXP{-} on a
negated numeral with it; so a coercion that throws an exception stops the
program.
A signed constant at a number type of \library\ is converted from its exact
value on both implementations, outside the coercion, so that no coercion from a
numeral type receives a sign.
The interpreter, which has no static types, applies a coercion from a numeral
type at the place's first evaluation, with the four numbers bound as values of
type \EXP{\mathbb{Z}}, and keeps its result for the place; it refuses a numeral
only when the place is evaluated: one outside an integer type's range, one at a
type that declares no coercion from the numeral's type or whose coercion's
\KWD{where} clause the numeral does not meet, a negated numeral at a type
without a prefix \EXP{-}, a folded constant at a type of a program's own
without a coercion from the constant's default type, and a numeral bound to a
variable declared of a numeral type.
It converts a numeral that rounds to an infinity of \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} or
\EXP{\mathbb{R}32} into that infinity with no error (row~967); it converts a
numeral at a parameter of the declaration that a call chooses, at a variable or
a field of a declared type and at a declared return type, but not one passed
through a tuple or a varargs parameter (rows~395 and~511).

load_exception_contains=Type mismatch binding 300
(* A coercion's where clause over the numeral's four numbers refuses a numeral outside it: 300 at a byte type. *)

value object Byte(b: ZZ32)

## 6. Sentences made false

The rung's build makes these false beyond what the patch already did (the probe's section 18 lists the patch's); rung T rewrites `revival-numerals` in place, so the gather checks that its new text holds these:

- `Specification/appendices/changes.tex:5185-5190`, `revival-numerals`' Effect: "The compiled code applies a program's coercion from a numeral type once for each place ... at a place whose type is a generic type of the program's own it applies the coercion at each evaluation of the place (row~957)." Now every numeral's place, at the library's types too, is one value: a JVM constant where the fold of the type's coercion ends in one, else a static final filled by one call of the coercion's method of the four numbers; at each evaluation only where the place's type names a type parameter (row 957, rewritten). A coercion that spawns still fails the class's load (row 971), which the Effect does not name.
- `changes.tex:5196-5200`: "both give a program's coercion a negative constant with its sign ... the compiled path as a negative numeral (row~961)": the compiled path applies the type's own minus to the coercion of the magnitude, once with the coercion (the patch and step 4).
- F-79 (`explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md:76`): the numeral types "value objects ... whose fields are the four numbers, and each of the eight number types converts from them with an `=` pair both ways", and "the prelude's `IntLiteral` and `FloatLiteral`": both gone (the patch).
- F-342 (`FACTS.md:161`): "`IntLiteral` and `FloatLiteral` are written in a program only as a parameter's type"; the selector keeps "the numeral's type" now `NaturalNumeral[\1,10,7\]` (row 963, rewritten).
- F-345 (`FACTS.md:287`): the specification's field numerals, for after rung T.
- The skill's `references/revival-changes.md`, "Numbers": "Its body reads the numeral's getters `digits`, `fractionDigits`, `radix` and `digitValue`." and "Until the switch-over, a compiled program writes `coerce(x: IntLiteral)` or `coerce(x: FloatLiteral)`."; "`Number` declares nothing (P-165). Each of the eight number types, and the two numeral types, declares its own `asFloat`".
- `references/compiler.md`, "What the code generator does": "It runs a program's own `coerce` from a numeral once for each place ..., except at a generic type (below)." Now every place's coercion, the library's too, is folded or run once by its method. "Traps of the compiled path": "At a program's own generic type, a numeral's coercion runs at each evaluation (ledger row 957)" (now only where the type names a type variable); "A negative constant at a program's own number type reaches its coercion with its sign ... Write `NOT (u = 0)`." (`u = 0` is `false` too, 973); "A negative constant ... reaches its `coerce(x: NaturalNumeral)` with its sign (ledger row 968)" (false).

Not run; for the gather to check on the merged tree.
- `Specification/basic/objects.tex:41-46`: "Most objects with simple standard types, such as booleans, numeric literals, ... are value objects" (the Working Draft's). Not false: a numeral denotes a value of a number type. Unchanged.
- `Specification/fortress/preamble.tex:54-64`, the front matter's paragraph on the revision: not made false. Unchanged.
- Rung A's section names the skill's sentences; none is the specification's.

content.content:
Every numeral has a \emph{numeral type} of its own, which exists only when the
program is compiled: no value of a numeral type exists when the program runs.
The static arguments of a numeral type are the numeral's \emph{four numbers}:
the number $n$ of its digits, leading zeros among them;
the number $m$ of its digits after the radix point, which the type of a numeral
without a radix point leaves out, $m$ being $0$;
its radix $r$;
and $v$, the value of its digits, with the radix point deleted, interpreted in
radix $r$.
Each of the four is a natural number, of any size.
A numeral containing only digits has the type
\EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n,r,v\rrbracket},
and a numeral containing a radix point has the type
\EXP{\TYP{RadixPointNumeral}\llbracket{}n,m,r,v\rrbracket}.
So \EXP{3.125} has the type
\EXP{\TYP{RadixPointNumeral}\llbracket{}4,3,10,3125\rrbracket},
\EXP{007} the type \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}3,10,7\rrbracket}, and
\EXP{3000000000} the type
\EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}10,10,3000000000\rrbracket}.
\Library\ declare the two numeral types below the trait \TYP{Numeral}, which
extends \TYP{Number} and has no static parameters: \TYP{NaturalNumeral} below
\TYP{AnyNaturalNumeral} and \TYP{RadixPointNumeral} below
\TYP{AnyRadixPointNumeral}, two traits that extend \TYP{Numeral} and exclude
each other.
None of these traits declares a method.
\note{Can the type \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n, 10, v\rrbracket}
have any value other than what you get from evaluating the corresponding literal?

What is the relationship between \EXP{\TYP{Literal}\llbracket{}v\rrbracket}
and \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n, 10, v\rrbracket}?

We need to describe the \TYP{Numeral} type hierarchy.
All the numeric/numeral types should be defined and their relations to each other given.
And a reference to where that is done should be appear in this section (probably at the beginning of the section).
}

\note{Ought we discuss digit-group separators here?
Or is that just part of lexical structure?
(I think we intend that a numeral consisting of digits and digit-group separators has
type \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n,10,v\rrbracket}
for appropriate values of \VAR{n} and \VAR{v}.)}

The radix of a numeral is ten, unless its digits are followed by an underscore
and a radix indicator (\secref{numerals}), which give its radix $r$; such a
numeral has one of the same two numeral types, with its radix as the static
argument $r$.
So \EXP{\mathtt{deadc}_{16}} has the type
\EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}5,16,912092\rrbracket}.

A numeral is converted where it stands, into the type that its place fixes,
and not before, because, as in common mathematical usage,
we expect numerals to be polymorphic.
For example, consider the numeral \EXP{3.1415926535897932384};
converting it to a floating-point number before its place is known
may lose precision.
If that numeral is used where a floating-point interval is expected,
it is better to convert it directly to an interval.
Therefore, numerals have their own types as described above.
This approach allows library designers to decide how numerals should
interact with other types of objects by defining coercion operations
(see \secref{coercion} for an explanation of coercion
in Fortress).
\Library\ define coercions
from numerals to integers (for simple numerals)
and rational numbers (for compound numerals).
In \library, each of the eight number types (\secref{basic-rationals}) declares
a coercion from \TYP{NaturalNumeral}, and \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}, \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}
and \EXP{\mathbb{R}32} declare one from \TYP{RadixPointNumeral}, each generic
over the four numbers, as \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} declares
\EXP{\KWD{coerce}\llbracket\KWD{nat} n,\KWD{nat} r,\KWD{nat} v\rrbracket(x\COLON \TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n,r,v\rrbracket)}.
The parameter of such a coercion has no value: its body computes the type's
value from the four numbers, which it reads as values, integers of type
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}} (\secref{natparams}).
The conversion is exact into the five integer types (\secref{basic-integers})
and \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}, and rounds once, to the nearest value of the type, into
\EXP{\mathbb{R}64} and \EXP{\mathbb{R}32}.
At a numeral, the compiler instantiates the coercion at the numeral's four
numbers and evaluates it: a value that the Java Virtual Machine holds as an
\texttt{int}, a \texttt{long}, a \texttt{float} or a \texttt{double} is a
constant of the compiled code, and any other value, as one of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}}
or \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}, is made once for the place where the numeral stands, so
that every evaluation of that place yields the same value.

A place \emph{fixes a type} for a numeral when the type declared there declares
a coercion from the numeral's type, as each number type of \library\ does and a
type of a program's own may.
The declared type of a variable, a field or a parameter, and the declared
return type of a functional, are such places, the parameter types of the
declaration that a call invokes among them (\secref{resolving-coercion}).
There the numeral is converted into that type, from its exact value:
so \EXP{q\COLON\mathbb{Q} = 0.1} binds the rational \EXP{1/10},
\EXP{r\COLON\mathbb{R}64 = 0.1} the floating-point number nearest to it, and
\EXP{n\COLON\mathbb{N}32 = 5} the natural number 5.
It is a static error if the numeral's value lies outside the range of that
type, or rounds to an infinity there.
Where nothing fixes a type, as where a variable is declared without a type, or
a parameter has the type \TYP{Any}, \TYP{Object} or \TYP{Number} or a type
parameter declared without a bound, the numeral is converted into its
\emph{default}: a numeral without a radix point into \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, or into
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} or \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} when its value does not fit in the
narrower type, and a numeral with a radix point into \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}.
So \EXP{x = 3} binds \VAR{x} as a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32},
\EXP{\VAR{bigN} = 3000000000} binds \VAR{bigN} as a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} and
\EXP{y = 0.5} binds \VAR{y} as an \EXP{\mathbb{R}64};
\EXP{x \sequiv z} is \VAR{true} for \EXP{z\COLON\mathbb{Z}32 = 3};
and for \EXP{\KWD{object}\;\TYP{Cell}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket(x\COLON{}T)},
\EXP{\TYP{Cell}(3)} is a \EXP{\TYP{Cell}\llbracket\mathbb{Z}32\rrbracket}.
\secref{numeral-default} says where else a numeral takes its default, as where
several numerals fix one type parameter, and how a numeral whose conversions
tie is read.
The default applies to a numeral, and to a static expression of numerals once
it is folded (\secref{static-expr}), never to an expression of a numeral type.

A type of a program's own receives a numeral as the number types of \library\
do, through its own coercion from the numeral's type, generic over the four

do, through its own coercion from the numeral's type, generic over the four
numbers, whose body computes the type's value from them.
So the Working Draft's floating-point interval can receive
\EXP{3.1415926535897932384} without rounding it first to a floating-point
number:
\begin{Fortress}
\(\KWD{object}\:\TYP{Interval}(\VAR{lo}\COLON\mathbb{R}64, \VAR{hi}\COLON\mathbb{R}64)\)\\
{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{coerce}\llbracket\KWD{nat} n,\KWD{nat} m,\KWD{nat} r,\KWD{nat} v\rrbracket(x\COLON \TYP{RadixPointNumeral}\llbracket{}n,m,r,v\rrbracket) =\)\\
{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(    \TYP{Interval}(\VAR{roundDown}(v, r, m), \VAR{roundUp}(v, r, m))\)\-\-\\\poptabs\poptabs
\(\KWD{end}\)\\[4pt]
\(\VAR{iv}\COLON\TYP{Interval} = 3.1415926535897932384\)
\end{Fortress}
where \VAR{roundDown} and \VAR{roundUp}, functions of the program, round
$v/r^m$ down and up to an \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}.
A numeral at a place whose type is a type of a program's own that declares no
coercion from the numeral's type is a static error: coercion does not chain
(\secref{coercion}), so the numeral is not converted into its default first.
The coercion receives the four numbers of a numeral as written.
A numeral as written under the prefix operator \EXP{-}, as \EXP{-3}, is that
operator of the type applied to the coercion's result for the numeral, so a type
without that operator refuses it; any other static expression of numerals alone
is folded first (\secref{static-expr}) and reaches the type only through the
type's coercion from the folded constant's default type, as \EXP{1/2} through a
coercion from \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}, and a type without that coercion refuses it.
A coercion may restrict the four numbers by a \KWD{where} clause that compares
them; a numeral whose four numbers do not meet it is a static error at that
type, as \EXP{300} is at a byte type whose coercion is
\EXP{\KWD{coerce}\llbracket\KWD{nat} n,\KWD{nat} r,\KWD{nat} v\rrbracket(x\COLON \TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n,r,v\rrbracket)\;\KWD{where}\;\{v < 256\}}.
At each place where such a numeral stands, the coercion is applied once, with
the type's prefix \EXP{-} where the numeral is negated, not at each evaluation
of the place, so that the numeral there denotes one object, as a string literal
does: two evaluations of one place yield the same object, and each place has its
own application of the coercion.
A numeral type is written in a program only as the type of a parameter, of a
coercion or of an operator, never as the type of a variable, a field or a
functional's result, nor as a static argument, nor as a type that a trait or an
object extends; so the constants \VAR{pi} and \VAR{e} of \library\ are values
of \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}.
\revision{revival-numerals}{The Working Draft of February 2011 said that
numerals are not directly converted to any of the number types, and so gave a
numeral where nothing fixes a type its own type; it said nothing of when a
coercion from a numeral type is applied.
The revival decided on 8~November 2026 that a numeral is converted where it
stands: where its place fixes a type, into that type, and elsewhere into the
default above; that a numeral type is written only as a parameter type; and
that a negated numeral reaches a type of a program's own as the type's prefix
\EXP{-} on the coercion's result.
It decided on 9~November 2026 that every number type, of \library\ and of a
program, receives a numeral through a coercion generic over the four numbers,
which the compiler instantiates at the numeral and folds, and that a numeral at
a place denotes one value, made once, the same on both implementations.
The interpreter, which has no static types, applies the coercion at the place's
first evaluation and refuses a numeral only there (\secref{revival-numerals}).
The text this replaces, the revival's own of 29~September 2026
(\secref{revival-numeral-type}), named the type of an integer numeral
\TYP{IntLiteral}, the name that the compiled path's own library gave it.}


\marginnote{What is an ``integer'' in this context?}
In Fortress, dividing two integers using the $/$ operator produces
a \emph{rational number};\marginnote{Not if the second integer is 0.}
this is true regardless of whether
the integers are of type $\mathbb{Z}$ (or \txt{ZZ}),
$\mathbb{Z}64$ (or \txt{ZZ64}), $\mathbb{N}32$ (or \txt{NN32}), or
whatever.  Addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division of rationals
are always exact; thus values such as \EXP{1/3} are represented exactly in
Fortress.

\note{We should give an example with a radix specifier.}
Numerals containing a radix point are actually rational
literals; thus \EXP{3.125} has the rational value \EXP{3125/1000}.
The quotient of two integer literals is a static expression
(described in \secref{static-expr}) whose value is rational.
Similarly, a sequence of digits with a radix point followed by the symbol
$\times$ and an integer literal raised to an integer literal,
such as \EXP{6.0221415 \times 10^{23}}
is a static expression whose value is rational.
If such static expressions are mentioned as part of a floating-point
computation, the compiler performs the rational arithmetic exactly and then
converts the result to a floating-point value, thus incurring
at most one floating-point rounding error.
But in general rational computations may also be performed at run time,
not just at compile time.
\revision{revival-numerals}{The revival decided on 8~November 2026 that an
expression of numerals and operators alone is folded exactly into a signed
constant before the static check, on both implementations
(\secref{static-expr}): so \EXP{x = 7/2} binds the \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} \EXP{7/2},
\EXP{1/2 = 0.5} is \VAR{true}, and the constant is rounded at most once where
a floating-point type is declared, since at a number type of \library\ it is
converted from its exact value; a type of a program's own receives it through
its coercion from the constant's default type.}
\note{This specifies too much about the implementation:
I don't think we should mention a compiler at all, except perhaps as informal discussion.
In particular, wouldn't it be correct if this arithmetic were actually deferred and
performed exactly at run time?}

such that $p \over k$ and $q \over k$ are integers

The compiled type checker does not apply the rule that a numeral type is written
only as a parameter type to the libraries' own files.
A numeral type declares no \EXP{=} with a number type, so a numeral compared by
\EXP{=} with a number of a type that declares no \EXP{=} with the numeral's
default type meets the top-level \EXP{=} of \library, whose parameters are of
type \TYP{Any} and which takes the numeral at its default: the interpreter answers \EXP{u = 0} \VAR{false}, and
\EXP{u \neq 0} \VAR{true}, for a zero \VAR{u} of \EXP{\mathbb{N}32},
\EXP{\mathbb{N}64} or \EXP{\mathbb{R}32}, none of which declares \EXP{=} with
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} (rows~966 and~973 of the revival's gap ledger; the
expected failure \nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/tests/XXXNumeralEqualsNumberWalk.fss}
asserts \VAR{true}), and whether \EXP{u = 0} is \VAR{true} is open; the compiled
path's own library declares no \EXP{=} over \TYP{Any}, and declares \EXP{=} and
\EXP{\neq} on each integer type with an operand of that type, into which the
numeral is converted, so that there \EXP{u = 0} is \VAR{true} and
\EXP{u \neq 0} \VAR{false} for a zero \VAR{u} of \EXP{\mathbb{N}32}.
The implementations depart from the text in these further ways, each with its
row of the revival's gap ledger: the interpreter runs the operator of
\EXP{\mathbb{R}64} where a floating-point numeral stands to the left of an
\EXP{\mathbb{R}32} (row~958); the interpreter loads and runs a program that writes a numeral type as a type that an object or a trait extends, or as a static argument (row~974); a numeral with a radix point keeps only one of
its leading zeros in its digit count, as the parser gives the numeral to both
implementations (row~960); the compiled path keeps a numeral's own type,

\KWD{typecase} (row~963); at a place whose type names a type parameter of its

content.content: - P-148 **The checker's speed comes right after its correctness in priority: a rung that changes the compiled checker also makes the change fast.** The rung times the checker before and after its change. It first makes the change correct. Then, in the same rung, it makes the new code fast, without changing which programs the checker accepts or refuses. So no optimization is left to be done by hand after the landing. Why: the checker must stay usable as it grows. Some slowdown is fine, but new checks have made it orders of magnitude slower, so that the checker ran past the time limit of the batch gate's count stage, and rungs could not land. The timing is a smoke test: one run of each tree, to catch a slowdown of several times; a small difference is noise. The `fortress-repo` skill (`compiler.md`, "The checker's time") gives the steps, their commands and what the rung reports.

content.content:
# Writing a test

**gated test**
: Test that the gate's suites run.

**green**
: Harness's report on a test that JUnit counts as passed.

**red**
: Harness's report on a test that JUnit counts as failed.

**`XXX` test**
: Gated expected failure. It asserts the answer that the specification gives, and fails today. The harness reports it green while it fails, and red when the defect is fixed.

## A test program

A test program has this form:

    component Name
    export Executable

    (* declarations *)

    run(): () = do
        assert(f(2), 4, "f(2)")
    end

    end

- `(*)` starts a comment to the end of the line. It cannot hold `*)`: the parser ends the comment there and refuses the program. `(* ... *)` comments nest.
- A compiled test with a `run` key ends `run()` with `println("PASS")`, unless a `run_out` key checks its output (below).
- Under walk, `assert(x, y, msg)` checks that `x` equals `y`. It and `=/=` call a type's own `=` only if the type extends a `FortressLibrary` trait that declares `=`, such as `Equality` (ledger row 807). Otherwise they compare by `SEQV` (`revival-changes.md`, "Traits and objects"). If a type `P` has its own `=`, make `P` extend `Equality[\P\]`, or write `assert(x = y, msg)`. The compiler's library declares the two-value `assert` only for `ZZ32`, `String` and `Character`; its `assert(flag, msg)` takes any `Boolean`.
- Do not name a variable or a parameter after a functional method of the library, such as `big`, `even`, `numerator` or `shift`. The disambiguator, the phase that binds names, refuses it: "Variable even is already declared."
- A test of run-time arithmetic or concatenation needs a variable operand, not a literal, because an expression of literals alone folds before the run (`revival-changes.md`, "Numbers").

## Where a test goes, and how it passes

Interpreter (walk): write `ProjectFortress/tests/Name.fss`, whose component is `Name`.

- Every `.fss` file there is gated, with no `.test` file needed.
- It is green if it throws no exception, exits 0, and neither its standard output nor its standard error contains `fail` or `FAIL`. A longer word counts too: `failure` fails the test. Only a file whose name contains `QuickCheckTest` is exempt.
- An api that it imports, and a helper component, go in `ProjectFortress/test_library/`. In `tests/`, a helper would run as a test.
- The harness skips files whose names end in `Syntax.fss`, `DynamicSemantics.fss` or `Satisfiability.fss`, or contain `GenomeUtil`.
- For a refusal at load, put `Name.test` beside `tests/Name.fss`, with `load_exception_contains=<message>`. A plain test is green if walk refuses the program at load as named. A failure while the top-level variables are initialised counts as a refusal. An `XXX` test with such a `.test` file is green if the program loads and runs clean.

Compiled: write `Name.fss` and `Name.test` in the compiled test folder that holds tests of its kind:

- `library_tests/`: the compiler's library. A test of the interpreter's library is an interpreter test (above).
- `parser_tests/`: the parser.
- `compiler_tests/`: the rest, beside the team's numbered `CompiledN` tests.
- `other_compiler_tests/`: the team's compiled tests that do not fit the `CompiledN` series, by the comment in `OtherCompilerJUTest.java`. Put no new test there.

The `.test` files are the whole list of tests: a `.fss` that no `.test` file names never runs. A `.test` file is a Java property file. It names the commands to run and the checks on their output, as lit's RUN and CHECK lines do:

    tests=Name                 the component(s) it drives; without it, the .test file's own name
    compile | link | typecheck each present command is one JUnit case; link compiles, then links
    run                        run the linked program in a subprocess (bin/fortress run)
    <command>_<stream>_<check>=text
                               command: compile, link or run; stream: out, err or exception;
                               check: contains, does_not_contain, equals, matches,
                               WIcontains (containment with runs of whitespace collapsed)

A `run` fails if the program exits non-zero or a `run_*` check fails. With no `run_out` check, its output must contain `pass` or `PASS`. With `run_exits_nonzero=true`, the run must exit non-zero, as a program whose class fails to load does. The `run_*` checks, and the `PASS` check where no `run_out` check is given, still apply. For example:

    tests=EqualityRung1
    link
    run
    run_out_WIcontains=PASS

## How `XXX` works

- Under walk, an `XXX` test is `tests/XXXName.fss`, whose component is `XXXName`. With no `.test` file, it is green when it fails as a plain test would.
- In the compiled test folders, the `XXX` prefix of a `.test` file's name applies to every command that the file drives: each must fail. So a defect at run time, whose link succeeds, needs two `.test` files ("Writing an `XXX` test").
- An unmet `run_*` check makes a run test red, whatever the prefix.
- The harness reports any link or compile exception of a component whose name contains `XXX` as expected, whatever the `.test` file's name. Only an unmet key of that command makes it red.
- An `XXX` compile test with a `compile_err_contains` key, whose program compiles, reports "Saw wrong failure", which is red.
- A green `XXX` test prints `Saw expected failure` or `OK Saw expected exception`.

## How a defect is recorded

Record every defect that you measure in one of three ways, and say in your report which:

1. Your change repairs it: an assertion in your plain gated test. It needs no `XXX` stage.
2. It is deferred, and the specification settles it: a gated `XXX` test that asserts the specification's answer. Write it in the change that measured the defect, even if a later change will repair it. If walk crashes on the program, still write the `XXX` test, unlike under 3: the harness counts the crash as the expected failure. A deferred defect of a program that the checker accepts and that then fails the JVM's verification (`VerifyError`), linkage or a range check at run time is one of these.
3. It is deferred, and the specification is silent or a conflict leaves it open (`exploring.md`): a test that asserts today's behaviour, and a row in the gap ledger (`records.md`). If no program can observe the defect, or no gated test can pass while it shows, as when walk crashes on the program, write the ledger row only. Its reproducer, the row's cell that names the test, is `none`, and its notes give the command and its output.

If your brief does not let you edit the original tree, say in your report which of the three the defect needs, and write a ledger row for it, whichever it needs. A probe that only measures and reports is an example. The change that next works there writes the test.

## The order: the test, its failure, the fix, the pass

1. Write the test, with a plain name. Write the essence of the defect as a clean, minimal program, not the shape in which a probe met it.
2. See the test fail through the harness (`harness-one.sh` or `junit.sh`, `tests-running.md`) on the base's code. Do this in a run that ends before you first build or compile your edit. Under walk, do it before you edit a library source that the test reads. If your tree already holds the fix, run the test through the harness on the old code, as `worktrees.md`, "Running the old code", says.
3. Make the fix. See the test pass in your last run after your last change of code.

The test needs no commit of its own. A test that comes with no fix, such as one that guards a behaviour that works today, has no failing run: see it pass through the harness.

In your report, quote two to five lines of the failing run, if there is one, and the passing line, each with its command. In an edit of the original tree, put every check into a gated test, never into a one-off script. A probe that only measures may use its own script. Assert a value with `assert` in an interpreter test. In a compiled test, assert it with `assert` (above), or print it and check it with a `run_out_equals` key. The harness checks both, so they are part of the suite's verdict.

An edit of prose in `Specification/` or `Documentation/` has no test. Check it as `specification.md`, "Changing the text: the revision form", says.

## Writing an `XXX` test

In a compiled test folder, name the component `XXXName`, in its file `XXXName.fss` and in its `component` line.

- For a refusal at compile time, write one `XXX` compile test, with `compile` and `compile_err_contains=<the refusal's message>`.
- For a code-generator wall (`compiler.md`, "What the compiled path cannot compile yet"), write `XXXName.test` with `tests=XXXName`, `compile` and `compile_exception_contains=<text of the exception>`.
- For a program that compiles and fails at run time, write two `.test` files over the component:
  - `NameLink.test`, a plain name, with `tests=XXXName` and `link`. It is red if the link reports static errors, but green on an exception.
  - `XXXName.test`, with `tests=XXXName` and `run`, and no `link`. Its run uses the plain file's link, so run the two files in one call of `junit.sh` or `fortress junit`, the plain one first.
  - The program prints `REACHED` in `run()` before the part that fails. The `XXX` file checks it with `run_out_contains=REACHED`, or with `run_out_does_not_contain=REACHED` if the run dies before `run()` prints. Never use `run_out_contains=PASS`.
  - Example: `compiler_tests/XXXBoxDotSpellingsRungW.test` and `BoxDotSpellingsRungWLink.test`.

Show the first `XXX` test that your change adds, and only the first, working through the harness (`harness-one.sh`, `junit.sh` or `fortress junit`), from its place in a gated test folder. A direct compile and run does not show this. Run it twice:

1. As it is: the harness must report an expected failure.
2. Changed for one run so that the defect does not show, then restored: the harness must report it red. For example, add the missing declaration to the test program, set the expected string to what the run prints, or, in a run-time pair, remove the part that fails.

## Promoting an `XXX` test

If your change fixes a defect that has a gated `XXX` test, the fix turns that test red. To find such a test, search the gap ledger (`records.md`): a row's reproducer names it. Also list the `XXX` files: `git ls-files 'ProjectFortress/*XXX*'`. Then promote it:

1. Before you edit the code, remove the prefix: give the test a plain name by its topic. Rename each file with `git mv` (`committing.md` gives the commit), or with `mv` if the file is not committed yet. Rename each `XXX` name inside: the `component` line, and in a compiled test the `tests=` lines and keys. Change a run-time pair as below.
2. See the plain-named test fail through the harness on the base's code, as "The order", step 2, says.
3. Make the fix and see the test pass.

A run-time pair keeps its three files, renamed without `XXX`. For example, `compiler_tests/NatRtTask` was promoted so in `fd5cb4864`:

- `Name.fss`, with `component Name`. The program asserts its values, then prints `PASS` last.
- `NameLink.test`: `tests=Name` and `link`.
- `Name.test`, in place of `XXXName.test`: `tests=Name`, `link`, `run` and `run_out_contains=PASS`.

## Names, comments, citations

- Name a test by its topic. Give it one comment line that says what it checks, with no pointer to a record.
- In a test, cite the specification by file and section or entry, never by line: `opr-overview.tex, subsection "GCD, LCM, and CHOOSE Operators"`. In the library chapters, name the entry too: `basic-integers.tex, section "Integers", opr CHOOSE`.
- If your change breaks a line of a test that the team wrote, respell the line and keep the value that it checks. Keep every assertion. List each line's before and after in your report.
- If your change touches mutable state, a field, an `atomic` block or library code that writes shared state, run its checks at one thread and at four. The same holds for the Java of tasks, transactions or the class loader. `harness-one.sh`, `junit.sh` and the suites force four threads. For one thread, run the program directly with the prefix `FORTRESS_THREADS=1` (a compiled program: `compiler.md`, "Running"), and check its exit code and output.

## 7. The homes, the ledger and the sibling sites

The worker's defects are each recorded as its section 11 says, except row 971, now home 2 (fix 2). The join range defect is home 1. `ledger.py find` for words of the change: rows 82, 314, 316, 442, 514, 581, 652, 691, 694, 769 and 959 are open and quote messages or notes that name the prelude's `IntLiteral`, which the patch deleted; their defects are not the numerals' and each message needs measuring again, so they are left for the gather. Sibling sites: the range check's other callers (`Functionals.scala:1239`, the argument positions) refuse a join argument by "not applicable"; the walk path refuses at run time; `Library/CompilerLibrary.fsi:43` and `CompilerLibrary.fss:93` keep comments that name `IntLiteral`, in the prelude, which goes at the switch-over.

## 8. The report and the record
## 9. Competing names and the failure mode

No other file of `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/` or of the test folders declares `NumeralCoercionFold`, a method named with `№`, `numeral$init`, or my tests' components. Failure modes: the fold turns a native that raises into no constant, and the place then raises at class load, loud; walk's `exactAt` wraps an integer only after `inRange` refused it out of range (program 5); the prelude's `NN64` coercion raises outside its range. My fix turns three crashes (the code generator's, the desugarer's and a `NoClassDefFoundError` at run time) into static refusals, the specification's answer.

content.content:
Each of the five integer types coerces from \TYP{NaturalNumeral} too.
A coercion from a numeral type is generic over the numeral's four numbers, the
static arguments of its type, as
\EXP{\KWD{coerce}\llbracket\KWD{nat} n,\KWD{nat} r,\KWD{nat} v\rrbracket(x\COLON \TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n,r,v\rrbracket)},
and computes the type's value from them (\secref{literals}): exactly into the
integer types and \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}, and with one rounding, to the nearest value
of the type, into \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} and \EXP{\mathbb{R}32}.
Since no value of a numeral type exists when a program runs, a numeral type
declares no \EXP{=} with a number type, and no number type declares one with a
numeral type.

Every other conversion between number types is written explicitly;
in particular, a conversion into \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} from
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, \EXP{\mathbb{N}64}, \EXP{\mathbb{N}32}, or \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}
is explicit, written \EXP{\VAR{asFloat}(x)} with the method that each of these types declares;
\TYP{Number} itself declares no conversion, and the numeral types declare no
\VAR{asFloat}.
\revision{revival-numerals}{Before this revision the passage named integer
numerals among the sources of the coercion into \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} only.
The revival decided on 8~November 2026 that each of the eight number types
converts from \TYP{NaturalNumeral}, and \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}, \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} and
\EXP{\mathbb{R}32} from \TYP{RadixPointNumeral}, and on 9~November 2026 that
each such coercion is generic over the numeral's four numbers, and that the
numeral types, of which no value exists when a program runs, declare no
\VAR{asFloat} and no \EXP{=} with a number type.}
\revision{revival-asfloat}{Before this revision the passage said that \library\ declare
\VAR{asFloat} on \TYP{Number}. Each number type now declares its own, and
\TYP{Number} declares none, so that a number type of a program's own need not
convert into \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}.}
\Library\ declare none of the constant traits.
An expression composed only of numerals and operators is folded, before the
static check and on both implementations, into a \emph{signed constant}, which
holds its value exactly and whose kind its operands give: computed from
numerals without a radix point and without a quotient, it is an integer,
written as an integer numeral or a negated one; computed from numerals without
a radix point with a quotient among its operations, it is a quotient, written as
the reduced quotient of two integer numerals; and computed from a numeral with a
radix point, it is written as a numeral with a radix point, or a negated one,
where its denominator divides a power of ten, and otherwise as the reduced
quotient of two numerals whose numerator has a radix point.
over the four numbers, for the number types of \library\ as for a program's;
only a numeral as written reaches such a coercion, and a signed constant at a

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""The record's tool: it owns the form of FACTS.md and POSITIONS.md and of
their two history files, and is the only way to write them.

An entry is one line under a permanent number, `- F-87 **Title.** Text.` in
explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md and `- P-48 **Title.** Text.` in
POSITIONS.md. A number is never reused or changed: a new entry takes the
highest number its file has ever used, plus one. An entry stands under the
nearest `## ` or `### ` heading above it, its section. Its title is its bold
opening, or where it has none, its opening words up to the first colon,
semicolon or full stop.

A pointer is another entry's number in the sentence that needs it, alone
(`It builds P-48.`) or with the first words of the target's title in quotes
(`It builds P-48, "A type parameter the arguments do not fix ..."`, or
`P-48 ("...")`). Quoted words must open the target's current title (`...` or
`…` marks words left out); when an entry is retitled, the tool rewrites them
in every entry that points to it, in the same call.

The history (FACTS-history.md, POSITIONS-history.md beside the record) holds,
under `### F-87`, one block per change, oldest first: one provenance line (the
UTC time from the clock, the kind of change, `from` each report section,
`commit`, `by`, then the note after a colon), and the line as it stood before
the change. The tool derives the kind: `added`, `rewritten`, `moved to "S"`,
`merged into F-n`, `F-n merged in`, `removed`, `noted`; the numbering wrote one
`numbered` block per entry. A retitle that refreshed other entries' pointer
words, or a merge that moved their pointers, says so in one more line of the
block (`pointer words refreshed in: F-12, P-48`).

A `noted` block, which `note` writes, leaves the entry as it is. It adds what
the entry's history lacks, such as the curator's messages behind a text kept
word for word, with their times, or a correction of an earlier block. It holds
no earlier line, and its note says what it adds, so it needs one. A gone entry
takes none: its last block stays `merged into` or `removed`. A noted block
that corrects an earlier block names it by its time, in the field after the
kind: `correcting the block of 2026-10-13 19:07Z`, or, where blocks of the
entry share that minute, `correcting the 2nd block of 2026-10-14 04:41Z`,
counted oldest first. The block corrected is never edited.

Every write takes a lock (flock on .record.lock beside the record), checks the
state it would leave, appends the history blocks first and then replaces each
record file in one step. A write is refused only for what would break the
store: a bad number, a pointer that does not resolve or whose words do not
open its target's title, a line break in an entry, no provenance (neither
`--from` nor `--note`; for a noted block, no `--note`), a correction that
names no block or more than one, two blocks for one entry in one call.
Never for size. The tool does not commit: commit the record file and its
history together.

usage: record.py COMMAND [ARGS] [PROVENANCE] [--root DIR]

  PROVENANCE: --from PATH#HEADING (repeatable; PATH from the repository root
  or from explorations/, HEADING held by exactly one heading of it, as doc:
  resolves one), --commit HASH (in HEAD's history), --by WHO, --note WHY.
  Each write needs --from or --note.

  add F|P --section TITLE FILE   a new entry from FILE's one line, numbered
      record.py add F --section 'Landed semantics' new.md --from 'compile-ladder/rung-x/REPORT.md#The fix' --by coordinator
  set N [FILE] [--section TITLE] entry N rewritten from FILE's line, or moved

- F-118 **A numeral's value reaches the compiled code intact, and the compiled path prints a large `NN32` or `NN64` value unsigned, but it cannot compare two `IntLiteral` values beyond `ZZ64`.** The code generator carries a numeral of its own type as an `int`, a `long` or its decimal string, by its exact bit length, and a numeral that the coercion desugarer types at a library number type as that type's constant (F-340). So on the compiled path `4294967295` and `18446744073709551615` keep their values, as walk does at `ZZ` and `ZZ64` (walk converts a numeral bound to `NN32` or `NN64`, F-341). The compiled path prints an `NN32` or `NN64` value above its type's signed half unsigned (F-313; test `compiler_tests/UnsignedPrintingCompiled`). It compares two `IntLiteral` values at `ZZ64`, so `lt(18446744073709551615, 5)` for `lt(a: IntLiteral, b: IntLiteral): Boolean = a < b` fails with `Not in range for ZZ64` (row 328), which no test pins; an untyped binding of such a numeral is a `ZZ`, its default (F-342). An `IntLiteral` arithmetic result of 64 bits or more also keeps its value compiled: observed in the report's probe, and no test gates it. Walk stops the same program at `x + x` with `IntegerOverflow`, since its fixed-width addition raises (F-132). Gated, for the numerals at `ZZ`, `ZZ64`, `NN32` and `NN64`, by `compiler_tests/IntLiteralWrapRepairR2`. Detail: `compile-ladder/repair-r2-literal-wrap/REPORT.md`, "The failure-mode question".

- F-262 **A numeral's sign does not reach its type on either path, so no overload on a numeral exponent's type can tell a positive exponent from a negative one, as in `x^16` and `x^(-16)`.** The numeral itself has no sign (`Specification/basic/lexical-structure.tex:1053-1080`). The checker types every integer numeral by its numeral type, `IntLiteral` under the compiler's prelude and `NaturalNumeral` under the one library (`Misc.scala:468-469`), before it converts it (F-342). Both paths fold `prefix -` on a numeral into a numeral node of negative value before the checker, and fold `^` of numerals by an integer numeral up to 4096 (F-339), but leave an integer base at a negative exponent: `10^16` is a numeral, and `10^(-16)` stays an operation whose exponent is a numeral (`compiler/desugarer/IntegerLiteralFoldingVisitor.java:292-302`). Walk's numeral is its default, an `Int` value read at `ZZ32` (F-74, F-341); a negative constant at a program's own type reaches its coercion as a `NaturalNumeral` of negative value under walk (row 968), and with its sign on the compiled path (row 961). By reading. Detail: `reviews/integer-power-fable-judgement.md` section 9.

component IntLiteralWrapRepairR2
export Executable

(*) The value a numeral of bit length exactly 32 or exactly 64 arrives with on
(*) the compile path.  CodeGen.forIntLiteralExpr split the numeral's BigInteger
(*) on bitLength() <= 32 and bitLength() <= 64, and bitLength counts no sign
(*) bit, so those two widths went through intValue() and longValue() and
(*) arrived wrapped negative: 4294967295 and 18446744073709551615 both became
(*) -1.
(*)
(*) Specification/basic/expressions/literals.tex, section "Literals" gives a numeral of
(*) digits the value of the numeral interpreted in radix ten, with nothing
(*) bounding it; Specification/basic-lib/basic-integers.tex, section "Integers", binary opr +, BOXPLUS and DOTPLUS and
(*) :400-401 give wrapping and saturating their own operator spellings and say
(*) the ordinary operations never need to wrap or saturate.
(*)
(*) Every expected value is computed at run time from numerals of bit length
(*) 16, 17, 31, 33 and 63, which no branch of the split ever mis-read, so a
(*) repair that returned a constant would not pass.
(*)
(*) The NN32 and NN64 checks pass before the repair as well as after: the
(*) getters asNN32 and asNN64 read the wrapped two's-complement pattern, which
(*) is the right unsigned value.  The NN64 check is here because the repair
(*) breaks asNN64 unless it learns to read the decimal string that a numeral of
(*) bit length 64 carries once the split is exact; the NN32 check guards a
(*) getter whose range check accepted every value before the repair.

run(): () = do
    (*) ZZ, the type the specification defines as all the finite integers.
    lo: ZZ = 65535                    (*) 2^16 - 1, bit length 16
    hi: ZZ = 65537                    (*) 2^16 + 1, bit length 17
    up: ZZ = 4294967297               (*) 2^32 + 1, bit length 33
    m32: ZZ = lo hi                   (*) 2^32 - 1, computed
    m64: ZZ = (lo hi) up              (*) 2^64 - 1, computed
    a32: ZZ = 4294967295              (*) 2^32 - 1, the numeral
    a64: ZZ = 18446744073709551615    (*) 2^64 - 1, the numeral
    assert(a32 = m32, "ZZ from the 32-bit numeral: " || a32.asString || " should be " || m32.asString)
    assert(a64 = m64, "ZZ from the 64-bit numeral: " || a64.asString || " should be " || m64.asString)

    (*) ZZ64, reached by the coercion ZZ64.coerce(x: IntLiteral) = x.asZZ64.

content.content:
- F-341 **Walk's numeral is its default, carrying the numeral's four numbers, and converts from them where its place fixes a type.** An integer numeral is a `ZZ32`, `ZZ64` or `ZZ` by its value, a radix-point numeral the `RR64` nearest its value, one value per site (`interpreter/evaluator/values/Numerals.java`). At a typed binding, an assignment, a field, a parameter, a declared return type and a coercion it converts through the place type's coercion from `NaturalNumeral` or `RadixPointNumeral`, called with the numeral object, one result per site and type; a numeral out of the type's range, or at a type with no coercion from it, is refused there when it runs; a store keeps its default alone. Dispatch fits it as it is at its own type or its default, then by its own type's coercions only, and reads a tie at the default; a type parameter that several numerals fix takes the narrowest default holding them all. So `q: QQ = 0.1` is 1/10, `y: RR64 = 0.5` is `SEQV` a computed 0.5, and `h = 0.5` is `true` for `h: QQ = 1/2`. Tests: `tests/NumeralTypesWalk.fss`, `NumeralOwnTypeWalk.fss`, `NumeralNoCoercionRefusedWalk.fss`, `NumeralAtReturnWalk.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-numeral-types/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why".

- F-346 **The library's `=/=` over `Any` meets a numeral at its default, against `e =/= e'` being `NOT (e = e')`.** Under walk `u =/= 0` is `true` for a zero `u` of `NN32`, `NN64` or `RR32`, and `q =/= 0.5` for `q: QQ = 1/2`, since `opr =/=(a:Any, b:Any) = NOT (a=b)` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:98`) has no pairs beside the `=` pairs (P-165), while `u = 0` and `q = 0.5` are `true` through those pairs; `basic/operators/opr-overview.tex` ("GCD, LCM, and CHOOSE Operators") makes `e =/= e'` `NOT (e = e')` (row 966). The compiled path until the switch-over answers `false` through the prelude's `=/=` on each integer type. Test: `ProjectFortress/tests/XXXNotEqualNumeral.fss` (an expected failure). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-literals-spec/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why".

content.content:
record.py set F-87 f87.md --from 'compile-ladder/rung-x/REPORT.md#The question' --note 'cut to the form'
  merge N --into M [FILE]        N removed, M rewritten from FILE (or kept),
                                 every pointer to N made a pointer to M
      record.py merge F-90 --into F-87 f87.md --note 'one fact, two entries'
  remove N                       N removed; refused while a pointer to it remains
      record.py remove P-131 --note 'evicted to the coordinator skill, references/briefing.md'
  note N [--correcting TIME]     a noted block in N's history, N unchanged; needs
                                 --note; refused when the history holds it already.
                                 TIME: 2026-10-13 19:07Z, or 2nd 2026-10-14 04:41Z
      record.py note P-25 --from 'positions-audit/full/evidence/corrections-c1.md#History lines the tool cannot write' --note 'his message behind the text: 2026-09-26T08:01:03.475Z, ...'
      record.py note P-7 --correcting '2026-10-13 19:07Z' --commit b87a17de5 --note 'that block names bc8902f47, ...'
  apply FILE                     many changes from one file, all or none (below)
      record.py apply chunk3.md --by 'consolidation chunk 3'
  check [--base COMMIT]          the store's checks; exit 1 on a failure
      record.py check --base cc9424c2a

An apply file holds, in any order: `## TITLE` or `### TITLE`, the section the
new entries below it go to (an existing entry stands under no heading, or
under its own section's, or the `## ` one that holds it); entry lines as they
should stand, `- F-87 ...`, or `- F-?1 ...` for a new entry, its placeholder
replaced by its number everywhere in the file; `move F-87 to SECTION`;
`remove F-90`; `merge F-91 into F-87`; `note F-87`, or `note F-87 correcting
TIME`, a noted block. Each may be followed by one indented provenance line of
its own:
`  from: PATH, "HEADING"; commit: HASH; by: WHO; note: WHY`. Blank lines and
`<!-- -->` comments are ignored. An entry line equal to the entry is skipped:
to add to its history, write `note F-87`. A note whose block the history holds
already, all but its time, is skipped too, so a file run twice writes nothing
twice. One call writes one block per entry, so an entry is noted, or changed,
once in a file.

check fails on: an entry line without its number, or a line under an entry
that continues it; a number on two lines; a number with no `numbered` or
`added` block, or one gone from its file whose last block is not `merged into`
or `removed`; a noted block that holds an earlier line, or whose `correcting`
names no earlier block of its entry, or more than one; a pointer to no live
entry, or quoted words that do not open the target's title; with --base, an
entry at COMMIT that is neither its line now nor the earlier line of a block
in its history (pointer words refreshed by the tool aside). It reports, without failing: the entries over 600 characters, the
entries without a bold title, and the `--from` paths and the report sections
an entry cites (`PATH`, "HEADING") that do not resolve.

The reads are facts-extract.sh's: `F-87`, `F-87+` (with the entries it points
to and that point to it), `history:F-87`, and the title queries, which fall
back to the former titles in the history.

content.content:
# Committing and pushing

**scratch**
: Files and folders that your work makes and `main` does not keep: logs, captured and raw run output, copies of tools, probe programs, lists and private caches folders.

Your brief says whether you commit and push, and on which branch. If it says nothing, commit on your current branch, and push it.

## What to commit

- Commit your change, its tests, your report if it is a file, and any reusable script.
- Commit what you write to the record, such as a ledger row, with the work that it records. A row's close follows the fix's commit (`records.md`).
- Keep scratch in your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
- In a fresh clone, `.claude/worktrees/` and `.claude/agents/` show as untracked, because the lines of `.git/info/exclude` that hide them are not in the clone. Do not commit them.
- Keep a copyrighted PDF or deck in `research/decks/`, which is gitignored. Cite it by its Wayback URL. Notes on it go in `research/extracts/`: your own summary, with brief attributed quotations.
- Put provenance and rationale in commit messages and reports, not in source comments.
- Name a model by its tier (Opus, Sonnet, Fable) in any text that you commit, commit messages included. Never write its model identifier, the API's name for the model, which starts with `claude-`.

## How to commit

Commit as you go, each commit in one command that names its paths:

    git add -- <paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <paths>

- The command commits only the paths that it names. Other agents may have uncommitted edits in your tree. Leave them alone.
- If you renamed a file with `git mv`, name its old path in `git commit` only, because `git add` refuses a path that no longer exists: `git add -- <new paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <new paths> <old paths>`.
- Never commit a copied directory, and never use `git add -A`.
- Before you commit more than a few hundred lines, stage them and read what you staged: `git add -- <paths> && git diff --cached --stat -- <paths>`.
- If the commit edits the original tree, say so in its message.
- End every commit message with this footer, exactly, whatever footer Claude Code suggests:

      Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
      Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB

  If your brief gives another session line, use it. If a commit that is already made has a footer that names a model, by any name or identifier, leave the commit as it is. Such a footer is not a defect: do not check for it, report it or list it.

## Pushing

Push after every commit, so that a lost container loses nothing.

- If you work on your own branch, push it: `git push -u origin <branch>` the first time, then `git push`. Your brief says how the branch reaches `main`.
- From a session in a cloud container, do not try to delete a branch on GitHub, or retry a refusal with another tool (the `cloud-container` skill, "Rules for every agent"). Removing a worktree does not delete its branch, which stays. Ask nobody in your report to delete a branch.
- If you work on `main`, other agents commit to it too. Push only your own commits:
  1. Run `git log origin/main..main`. Your commits are those whose hashes your own `git commit` printed.
  2. If it lists another agent's commit, run the command again shortly: that agent pushes right after it commits. If the commit stays, push nothing, and say so in your report.
  3. If it lists only your commits, push the three refs with this one command, and wait for it to end:

         git push --atomic origin main main:claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8 main:blinded-fable

     With `--atomic`, the three refs update together or not at all. Do not pipe the command into another command, since a pipe hides a refusal. A refusal shows as a line that starts with `!`, and as a non-zero exit. The last ref keeps `blinded-fable` current. If the container is lost, the platform rebuilds it from that branch.
- Push no branch that this section does not name, unless your brief names it.
- If a push is refused, push nothing more, and do not run it again. Report the refused ref and git's message.
